If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can name the difference between grinding for a grade and learning because they want to know, explain why curiosity matters for memory and for having something real to say, and pick one small way to feed their curiosity this week. Nobody is asked to share grades, college plans, or how much pressure they're under at home.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 6 minRabbit holes: turn and talk, share out
  2. 4 minGrind or curiosity?
  3. 4 minThe grind loop
  4. 6 minThe trivia experiment, and curious brains
  5. 10 minSomething to say: Riley, Nora, and you
  6. 5 minFeed one question
  7. 6 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Rabbit holes, grind or curiosity, the trivia experiment, the two seniors, and feed one question.

Before you teach
Grades still matter, and that's okay to say.

This lesson isn't anti-grades or anti-college. Students who need scholarships, or whose families have sacrificed for their education, can feel judged by "stop grinding" talk. Frame it as making room for both.

Don't ask about college lists or GPAs.

Comparing in a small circle is exactly the pressure this lesson is about. Keep examples general and invented.

Watch for students who are running on empty.

Some students describe a schedule with no slack at all, little sleep, or feeling numb about things they used to enjoy. That's worth a quiet check-in after advisory and a same-day note to a counselor if it sounds serious. Disclosures go to a counselor. No screening questions in the group.

Curiosity can look different.

For some students it's gaming lore, sneakers, cooking, a sport's stats, car repair, a faith question, or a younger sibling's homework. Treat all of it as real curiosity. The point is wanting to know, not the topic.

Be honest about admissions.

Say what the evidence supports: many admissions deans endorsed the Turning the Tide report asking for depth and genuine interest over long lists. Don't promise that curiosity gets anyone into a particular school.

Model it.

Share one thing you got curious about recently, outside your subject. Students take the permission more seriously when an adult goes first.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Money and time aren't equal.

Some students work after school, care for siblings, or can't afford camps and lessons. Curiosity doesn't need money: a library card, a question list, a free online course, a conversation with a grandparent. Keep every suggestion free.

Family expectations vary.

In some families, academic achievement is how love and sacrifice get honored. Don't set curiosity against family. Say students can carry both, and that a counselor can help with a family conversation if they want one.

Not every family has one path.

Some students are headed to college, some to work, the military, a trade, or a family business. Curiosity matters for all of them. Avoid making college the only finish line in your examples.

Neurodivergent students.

Students with ADHD often have intense, deep interests that school treats as distractions. Name those interests as curiosity. Students with a learning plan may already spend extra hours on schoolwork; protecting free time matters even more for them.

Identity and belonging.

Students of color, LGBTQ+ students, and students new to the country may follow curiosity about their own history, language or community. Treat that as real intellectual curiosity, not a side interest.

Language.

English learners may be curious about plenty and quiet in English. Let them write their rabbit-hole card in any language, or draw it.

What the research says

When people were curious about a trivia question, they remembered the answer better, and also remembered unrelated faces shown while they were curious. Brain scans showed the reward and memory systems working together.

Gruber, Gelman & Ranganath, Neuron, 2014

In a meta-analysis, intellectual curiosity predicted academic performance about as strongly as conscientiousness, on top of intelligence.

von Stumm, Hell & Chamorro-Premuzic, Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2011

Adolescence is a period of heightened sensitivity to novelty and reward and flexible goal pursuit, which researchers describe as an opportunity for learning and exploration.

Crone & Dahl, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2012; Dahl et al., Nature, 2018

Students at high-pressure schools often describe "doing school": managing grades and activities in ways that crowd out engagement and learning.

Pope, "Doing School", Yale University Press, 2001

Students at high-achieving schools have been identified as an at-risk group, with higher rates of anxiety, depression and substance use than national norms, linked partly to achievement pressure.

Luthar, Kumar & Zillmer, American Psychologist, 2020

A report endorsed by dozens of college admissions deans urged admissions to value meaningful, sustained engagement over long activity lists.

Making Caring Common, Harvard Graduate School of Education, Turning the Tide, 2016

Teens build initiative most in voluntary activities they care about, where they are focused and motivated at the same time.

Larson, American Psychologist, 2000
